title: The convex hull of a compact set in a finite real coordinate space

content.display_title: The convex hull of a compact set in a finite real coordinate space
content.one_sentence_role: Realizes the ordinary convex hull as a finite union of compact images of bounded-length convex combinations.
content.natural_language_statement: If $I$ is finite and $K\subseteq\mathbb R^I$ is compact, then $\operatorname{conv}(K)$ is compact. The set $K$ may be empty.
content.assumptions: The coordinate space is real and has finitely many coordinates. Only compactness of $K$ is assumed; no convexity or nonemptiness of $K$ is required.
content.conclusion: The ordinary convex hull itself is compact. No closure is added to the statement. In particular the conclusion includes $\operatorname{conv}(\varnothing)=\varnothing$.
content.proof_summary: Bound the length of every convex combination by the dimension plus one, then take the finite union of the corresponding compact images.

proof_steps.text:
Write $d=|I|$. For $0\le k\le d+1$, put

$$\begin{gathered}
\Delta_k=\{t\in\mathbb R^k:t_i\ge0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{k}t_i=1\},\\
F_k:\Delta_k\times K^k\longrightarrow\mathbb R^I,\qquad
F_k(t,x)=\sum_{i=1}^{k}t_ix_i,\\
C_k=F_k(\Delta_k\times K^k).
\end{gathered}$$

For $k>0$, $\Delta_k$ is closed and $0\le t_i\le1$, so it is compact in finite dimensions. For $k=0$, it is empty and hence compact. The finite product $\Delta_k\times K^k$ is compact, and $F_k$ is continuous as a finite sum of scalar multiplications. Thus every $C_k$ is compact.

Every $C_k$ lies in $\operatorname{conv}(K)$ by the defining property of convex combinations. Conversely, the affinely independent representation of a point in the convex hull provides finitely many points in $K$ with positive weights summing to $1$. An affinely independent family in a $d$-dimensional space has at most $d+1$ points: after choosing one point, its difference vectors are linearly independent and there are at most $d$ of them. Reindexing the representation by $1,\ldots,k$ puts the point in $C_k$ for some $k\le d+1$.

Thus

$$\operatorname{conv}(K)=\bigcup_{k=0}^{d+1}C_k.$$

The right side is a finite union of compact sets and hence compact. For $k=0$, the empty weight sum is $0$, so $\Delta_0$ is empty. If $K$ is empty, $K^k$ is empty for every $k>0$; therefore all the images are empty, and the same union proves the empty-set case.

content.lean_realization_notes: The finite dimension is used to bound the number of points in a convex representation. Compactness then comes from finitely many parameter spaces, not from an unrestricted union over all possible lengths.
